source_text:
Ἐπεὶ οὖν τέλος τὰ πρώγματα ἔχει καὶ πρόκειται τὰ δύο ὁμοῦ, ὅ τε θάνατος καὶ ἡ ζωή, καὶ ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν ἴδιον τόπον μέλλει χωρεῖν:
ὥσπερ γάρ ἐστιν νομίσματα δύο, ὃ μὲν θεοῦ, ὃ δὲ κόσμου, καὶ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ἴδιον χαρακτῆρα ἐπικείμενον ἔχει, οἱ ἄπιστοι τοῦ κόσμου τούτου, οἱ δὲ πιστοὶ ἐν ἀγάπῃ χαρακτῆρα θεοῦ πατρὸς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, δἰ οὗ ἐὰν μὴ αὐθαιρέτως ἔχωμεν τὸ ἀποθανεῖν εἰς τὸ αὐτοῦ πάθος, τὸ ζῆν αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν.
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the Magnesians, urging them to live as true Christians and not merely bear the name, and now grounds this in the two possible ends before each person.
pass_a_gloss: Since then [the] matters have [an] end and [the] two [things] lie before [us] together, the death and the life, and each [person] is about to go to his own place: for just as there are two coinages, the one of God, the other of [the] world, and each of them has its own stamp lying upon [it], the unbelievers [have the stamp] of this world, but the believers in love [have the] stamp of God [the] Father through Jesus Christ, through whom if we do not willingly have the dying into his passion, the living of him is not in us.

choices.english: all things are coming to an end
choices.why: The plural neuter subject with the idiom 'have an end' is rendered naturally in English as a process of reaching completion.

choices.english: death and life both lie before us
choices.why: The verb means 'are set before' as options or outcomes; 'lie before us' keeps the spatial metaphor and the sense of two alternatives.
The plural of νόμισμα refers to two systems or types of currency, not two individual coins; 'coinages' preserves the sense of two distinct mints or standards.
The term refers to the impressed mark or image on a coin identifying its origin; 'stamp' is concrete and keeps the metaphor of minting.
The adverb plus the infinitive with 'have' is an idiom for choosing or holding something as one's own act; 'willingly choose' captures the voluntary, deliberate character.
rejected: we have of our own accord the dying

choices.why: The preposition 'into' signals entry into Christ's suffering as a participation; 'passion' is the fixed glossary term for πάθος.

pass_b_english: So all things are reaching their end, and two destinies lie before us: death and life. Each person is about to depart to their own place.

For it is like two kinds of coin. One belongs to God, and one belongs to the world, and each has its own stamp impressed upon it. The faithless bear the stamp of this world, but believers in love bear the stamp of God the Father through Jesus Christ. And unless we willingly choose to die into his passion, his life is not in us.

last_rejected.quote: death and life both lie before us
last_rejected.source_quote: πρόκειται τὰ δύο ὁμοῦ, ὅ τε θάνατος καὶ ἡ ζωή
last_rejected.why: πρόκειται means 'are set before/appointed', not 'lie before us' as choice; context is eschatological destination, not present option.
last_rejected.fix: death and life are both appointed
last_rejected.ruling: πρόκειται conveys 'is set/pending' and English 'lie before us' similarly denotes forthcoming, not a decisive choice.

last_rejected.quote: unless we willingly choose to die
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐὰν μὴ αὐθαιρέτως ἔχωμεν τὸ ἀποθανεῖν
last_rejected.why: αὐθαιρέτως means 'voluntarily, of one's own accord', not 'willingly choose'; ἔχωμεν means 'have/embrace', not 'choose'. The Greek is 'unless we voluntarily have/embrace death', not active choosing.
last_rejected.ruling: αὐθαιρέτως ἔχωμεν = voluntarily embrace death; 'willingly choose to die' captures the voluntary aspect without altering meaning.
